Paṭṭadakal
------------------------------------------
India is dotted with temples, both ancient and modern.
The earliest temples could have been built with easily perishable materials like wood and hence have not survived the ravages of weather and time. Only when they were built in stone, they have lasted for centuries.
Some of the earliest of such temples are found in ऐहोऌए and पट्टदकल् (Bijapur district of Karnataka State). Situated on the left bank of the river Malaprabhā, the village पट्टदकल् is hardly four acres in area and is surrounded by a stone-wall, like a fort.
पट्टदकल्">A view of the temples at PaṭṭadakalIt is said that some of the kings of several dynasties—the Nandas, the Guptas, the Kadambas and the Coḷas—used to have their paṭṭābhiṣeka (coronation ceremony) here. Hence the name ‘Paṭṭadakal’.
Known by other names such as Hammīranagara, Paṭṭaśilāpura, Peṭirgala, Kisuvoḷal and Raktapura, पट्टदकल् was once a prosperous town. It was also the capital of the king Kīrtivarma of the Caḷukyan dynasty.
Along with ऐहोऌए (in the same district), पट्टदकल् is famous for its several old and big temples (ten in number), of which the following are more well-known: Mallikārjuna, Pāpanātha, and Virūpākṣa.
The Mallikārjuna temple is small and might have been built during the early part of eighth century. There are three sanctums for ब्रह्मा, विष्णु and शिव. Incidents from the epics have been carved on some of the pillars. The various images have a nice appearance.
The Pāpanātha temple is dedicated to शिव. It is in fairly good condition with the शिवलिङ्ग in the sanctum intact. Its architectural style is a mixture of the द्राविड (South Indian) and the नागर (North Indian). The outer wall on the south contains embossed figures of almost the entire रामायण.
The Virūpākṣa temple—also known as Lokeśvara temple—built by the queen Lokamahādevī (wife of the king Kīrtivarma, the second, and daughter of the हैहय king) during the early part of the 8th century A. D., is the biggest of the temple complex at पट्टदकल्. Apart from a prākāra or an outer wall, it has two main gates. Nandimaṇḍapa has been built separately. There are three structures for the Trimūrtis (Brahmā, विष्णु and महेश्वर) also. Figures depicting scenes from the Rāmāyaṇa, decorative windows and a squarish शिखर (of the drāviḍian style) are the other features.
Other temples in the complex are those of Kāśīviśveśvara, Saṅgameśvara, Gaḷaganātha, and Jambuliṅga.
Several stone edicts belonging to the period 8th and 9th centuries have been found at these temple sites.
The names of some of those involved in the construction of these temples have been inscribed here and there. Some of them are: Revaḍi Ovajja and Anivārita-guṇḍa (Sthapatis or architects); Ceṅgamma, Pullappan Nirmāṇadeva, Baladevayya and Deva Ārya (śilpis or sculptors); Acalan (nāṭyaśāstra pravīṇa, expert dancer).
The ऐहोऌए-बादामि-पट्टदकल् group of temples has been considered a great archaeological treasure and is being protected as such.
See also AIHOḶE and BĀDĀMI.

Pāṭaliputra
------------------------------------------
Also known as Pāṭaligrāma, Puppla-pura (Puṣpapura) and Kusumapura, it was an ancient city of great fame. गौतम बुद्ध seems to have visited it (which was a small village at that time) during अजातशत्रु’s reign and predicted a great future for it.
According to कौटिल्य’s Arthaśāstra (321 B. C.) it was the greatest city in the East even by the 4th century B. C.
It was the capital of the Mauryas and the Śuṅgas. Megasthanies (302-288 B. C.) has mentioned that it extended on the bank of the गङ्गा, defended by a wooden palisade flanked by 570 bastions and surrounded by a deep wide moat. It had 64 gates in all! It was also the capital of the kingdom of Magadha. Hiuen Tsang (A. D. 600-664) has described how the king Kālāśoka made it his metropolis.
It has been identified with the modern Patna city (capital of Bihar).

paṭṭinī cult
(‘the cult of a chaste wife’)
------------------------------------------
Associated with the cult of शक्ति or the Divine मोथेर्, cults of some minor goddesses also grew, either round them or independently.
Some of these goddesses were personifications of certain dreadful diseases like smallpox. They had to be specially appeased to be freed from these diseases. Some of them again, were human beings like द्रौपदी, the queen of the Pāṇḍavas, and those who committed सती (dying on the funeral pyres of their husbands) raised to the level of a divinity in course of time.
One cult that arose chiefly in Tamil Nadu was centred round Kannagi—the wife of Kovalan—a paragon of wifely virtues and chastity. It was called the पट्टिनी चुल्त्. (The word paṭṭinī seems to be a corrupted form of the Sanskrit word patnī or wife.)
The cult gradually spread from Tamil Nadu to Ceylon (now Sri Lanka).
An annual celebration with decoration and some sort of worship seems to be a characteristic of such cults.
